anyhow.whatItIs: anyhow, a library for the Rust programming language that reports program errors and adds a plain explanation of what was being done.
goodAt: Reporting failures from an app's own code with clear messages
Adding a note on which step failed, such as reading a file
notGoodAt: Defining exact error types that other code must check for; use thiserror for that.
anyhow.example: When the program cannot open a settings file, it reports that the settings file could not be opened, along with the reason.

assert_cmd.whatItIs: assert_cmd, a library for the Rust programming language that runs a built command-line program in a test and checks what it printed and how it exited.
goodAt: Testing a command-line tool the way a person or script would run it
Checking a program's exit status and its printed output together
notGoodAt: Testing one function inside the program; an ordinary unit test does that faster.
assert_cmd.example: A test runs the tool with a missing settings file and checks that it exits with an error and prints a hint on how to fix it.

axum.whatItIs: axum, a library for the Rust programming language that builds web servers: it matches each incoming request to the code that answers it.
goodAt: Web services that answer requests with JSON data
Reading request bodies, addresses and settings into typed values
notGoodAt: Pages people click through, with templates and forms; use a web app stack.
axum.example: When a phone app asks the service for a list of notes, axum sends the request to the code that loads them and returns them as JSON.

clap.whatItIs: clap, a library for the Rust programming language that reads the words and options typed after a command-line program's name.
goodAt: Turning a program's commands and options into typed values
Writing the help text and error messages for wrong options
notGoodAt: Full-screen terminal screens with menus and panels; that needs a terminal interface library.
clap.example: When someone types the tool's name with --help, they get a list of its commands and options without the developer writing that text by hand.

insta.whatItIs: insta, a library for the Rust programming language that saves a test's output to a file and fails the test when the output later changes.
goodAt: Checking large outputs, like a whole screen of text, without typing them out
Showing exactly what changed so a person can accept or reject it
notGoodAt: Deciding whether new output is right; a person still has to read each change.
insta.example: A test draws the app's main screen and compares it with the saved copy, so a moved column or missing line fails before anyone ships it.

js-sys.whatItIs: js-sys, a library for the Rust programming language that lets Rust compiled to WebAssembly use JavaScript's built-in objects, such as errors, arrays and JSON.
goodAt: Creating real JavaScript errors and objects from Rust code
Reading the keys and values of an object JavaScript passed in
notGoodAt: Web page features such as the document or fetch; a separate browser library covers those.
js-sys.example: When the Rust code rejects an input, it throws a normal JavaScript error that the web page's code can catch and read.

proptest.whatItIs: proptest, a library for the Rust programming language that tests code with many generated inputs and, when one fails, shrinks it to the simplest failing case.
goodAt: Checking a rule holds for every input, not just a few examples
Finding odd inputs a person wouldn't think to write down
notGoodAt: Checking one exact expected result; an ordinary example test reads more clearly.
proptest.example: A test tries thousands of made-up names and checks that each one the code accepts comes back out exactly as it went in.

ratatui.whatItIs: ratatui, a library for the Rust programming language that draws full-screen text interfaces in a terminal: lists, panels, tables and popups.
goodAt: Keyboard-driven apps that fill the terminal window
Laying out panels that adapt to the window's size
notGoodAt: Graphical windows with a mouse-first design; that needs a desktop app framework.
Simple commands that print a result and exit; a command-line parser alone is enough.
ratatui.example: A task list fills the terminal, the arrow keys move between tasks, and Enter opens one in a detail panel.

serde.whatItIs: serde, a library for the Rust programming language that converts data between saved text formats and the program's own data shapes.
goodAt: Reading settings and records saved in a text format
Writing the program's data out in a form other programs can read
notGoodAt: Storing data in a database; use a database library for that.
serde.example: When the program loads a saved order from a file, it turns the text into an order record the rest of the code can use.

serde-wasm-bindgen.whatItIs: serde-wasm-bindgen, a library for the Rust programming language that turns JavaScript objects into Rust data and back, for Rust compiled to WebAssembly.
goodAt: Reading an options object a JavaScript caller passes
Returning Rust results to JavaScript as plain objects and arrays
notGoodAt: Rejecting keys it doesn't expect; the code has to check those itself.
serde-wasm-bindgen.example: A web page passes { maxLength: 10 } to a function written in Rust, and the Rust code receives it as a typed settings record.

serde_json.whatItIs: serde_json, a library for the Rust programming language that reads and writes JSON, a text format for exchanging data.
goodAt: Reading JSON settings or web responses into Rust data
Writing Rust data out as JSON text
notGoodAt: Checking business rules by itself; the program needs its own checks.
serde_json.example: When a settings file arrives as JSON, the program reads it into a Rust record and reports a clear error if a required part is missing.

specta.whatItIs: specta, a library for the Rust programming language that writes the shape of a program's data into other programming languages, so both sides agree on it.
goodAt: Sharing Rust data shapes with the code that draws a website or desktop screen
Catching a mismatch between Rust data and the screen code that reads it
notGoodAt: Providing the actions a desktop app performs; use Tauri for that.
specta.example: A Rust part of a desktop app returns a list of saved files, and the screen code gets a matching shape, so it can show the list without guessing.

specta-typescript.whatItIs: Writes Rust data shapes, made with Specta, into TypeScript code that a screen can use.

tauri.whatItIs: Tauri, a toolkit for building desktop apps that show a web-style screen and run their logic in Rust, a programming language.
goodAt: Opening a desktop window that shows a web-style screen
Letting the screen call Rust code and get answers back
notGoodAt: Designing the screens for you; the web-style part needs its own code.
tauri.example: When a user clicks Export in a desktop app, a button on the screen runs Rust code that saves the file to the user's computer.

tauri-build.whatItIs: Adds the setup steps a Tauri desktop app needs when it is built.

tauri-specta.whatItIs: tauri-specta, a bridge that shares a Tauri desktop app's Rust actions and data shapes with its screen code.
goodAt: Keeping the desktop app's Rust actions and the screen code's data shapes matching
notGoodAt: Doing the real work of each action; that Rust code must be written separately.
tauri-specta.example: When a developer adds a Rust action that saves a note, the screen code gets a matching piece it can call, with the right kinds of input.

tempfile.whatItIs: tempfile, a library for the Rust programming language that makes short-lived files and folders and removes them when done.
goodAt: Holding temporary working files during a test or a data job
Removing test files once the test finishes
notGoodAt: Keeping files for later; save those to a folder you choose.
tempfile.example: A test writes a temporary order file, reads it back, and the file is removed when the test ends.

thiserror.whatItIs: thiserror, a library for the Rust programming language that helps define the program's own kinds of error, each with a clear message.
goodAt: Giving a library's errors clear names and messages
Letting other code tell one failure from another
notGoodAt: Deciding how to recover from an error; the code using the library does that.
thiserror.example: When a customer uploads a file that is not an order file, the error says so by name, not just 'something went wrong'.

tokio.whatItIs: tokio, a library for the Rust programming language that runs many jobs at once, such as handling web requests and reading files.
goodAt: Handling many web connections at once in a Rust server
Reading and writing files without stopping the rest of the program
notGoodAt: Providing the overall structure of an app; choose a framework separately.
tokio.example: When many people load a Rust web service at the same time, it can work on several requests at once instead of finishing one before starting the next.

toml.whatItIs: toml, a library for the Rust programming language that reads and writes settings files in the TOML format.
goodAt: Reading a program's settings file into typed values
Reporting the line where a settings file has a mistake
notGoodAt: Merging settings from several places; the program decides which source wins.
toml.example: When a settings file has a typo in a key name, the tool stops and names the key and the line it was on.

tower.whatItIs: tower, a library for the Rust programming language that wraps a server's request handling in reusable steps, such as time limits.
goodAt: Giving every request the same time limit or retry rule
Calling a server's routes directly in tests, without a network
notGoodAt: Answering web requests on its own; it works under a web framework such as axum.
tower.example: When a request takes longer than ten seconds, the service stops it and answers that it is busy instead of leaving the caller waiting.

tower-http.whatItIs: tower-http, a library for the Rust programming language with ready-made web server steps such as request ids, request logs and crash recovery.
goodAt: Giving each request an id and logging how it ended
Turning a crash in one request into an error reply instead of a dropped connection
notGoodAt: Deciding which code answers a request; that is the web framework's job.
tower-http.example: Every reply from the service carries a request id, and the log line for that request has the same id, so a support ticket can be traced.

tracing.whatItIs: tracing, a library for the Rust programming language that records what a program does step by step, and ties each record to the job it belongs to.
goodAt: Following one request's steps through a program that handles many at once
Recording the steps of a single job so they can be read later
notGoodAt: Saving or showing records on its own; use tracing-subscriber for that.
tracing.example: While a desktop app saves a document, the program records each step, so a developer can see where a failed save stopped.

tracing-subscriber.whatItIs: tracing-subscriber, a library for the Rust programming language that collects the records made by tracing and writes them out in a readable form.
goodAt: Sending a program's recorded steps to the screen or a file
Setting how much detail gets written out
notGoodAt: Making the records itself; the program's code has to mark each step.
tracing-subscriber.example: A desktop app can print each step of a save as it happens, with the time and the step's name, so the output reads like a timeline.

wasm-bindgen.whatItIs: wasm-bindgen, a library for the Rust programming language that lets Rust compiled to WebAssembly and JavaScript call each other, with TypeScript types for the JavaScript side.
goodAt: Offering Rust functions and classes to JavaScript code with typed signatures
Passing text, numbers and objects between Rust and JavaScript
notGoodAt: Packaging the result for npm by itself; wasm-pack runs it and writes the package.
wasm-bindgen.example: A web page calls slugify("Hello World") from an npm package, and the work runs as fast compiled Rust inside the browser.

wasm-bindgen-test.whatItIs: wasm-bindgen-test, a testing library for the Rust programming language that runs tests compiled to WebAssembly inside Node or a browser.
goodAt: Testing Rust code where JavaScript will actually run it
Checking the values and errors JavaScript receives from Rust
notGoodAt: Fast checks of plain logic; ordinary Rust tests run those without WebAssembly.
wasm-bindgen-test.example: A test calls the package's function with a JavaScript object and checks that a bad option comes back as an error with the right code.
